doc.title: Joe Temperley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Standards in Glasgow and hunting for American records
summary: Tunes played in the Glasgow club, and the effort of ordering scarce 78s such as Sing Sing Sing, compared with having everything on CD now.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What kind of tunes were you playing in this club in — was it Edinburgh you said?
In Glasgow, yeah. I don’t know. I think like “My Blue Heaven” and “Blue Skies” and you know those kind of standards.
Was there a sense that this music was coming out of America and that we wanted to get our hands on it? That records of it were something to search out for you guys?

Oh yes. It was very important. That was very important to search out records. Because they were very scarce and you didn’t see many 78s in those days. So when a new record came, a new record would be maybe Benny Goodman’s “Sing Sing Sing” and everybody would have to get a copy of “Sing Sing Sing.” You’d have to order it, it would have to come from London or somewhere, you know, it was a whole big operation. Nowadays you have everything on hand. The whole history of jazz is right there before you.
Right, yes. I mean I think of myself, I have maybe about 60 or 70 Duke Ellington CDs. In those days, the only Duke Ellington song I probably knew would be maybe “Take the A Train” or something.
